***
# Summary

An MR1 data package holds the data of one radar campaign (e.g. `CH_Sempach_2024`)
in a standardised, self-describing format: the
[Frictionless Data Package](https://datapackage.org). It consists of one CSV
file per table and a `datapackage.json` file that describes the tables (column
types, descriptions, units, and how the tables link to each other) and the
campaign (title, contributors, licence, embargo, location, period, ...).

Each campaign package is published as its own dataset on Zenodo, with its own
DOI. These campaign datasets are grouped in owner collections (e.g. all
campaigns of the Swiss Ornithological Institute) and in a community collection
(all BirdScan MR1 campaigns), so users can cite the level that matches their
study.

The workflow has 7 steps:

1.    Extract the data from the SQL database.

2.    (optional) Load the manual blind times.

3.    Describe the campaign in a metadata file.

4.    Create the data package.

5.    Validate the data package.

6.    Upload the data package to Zenodo.

7.    Group the published campaigns in collections.

***
# Before we get started

We first load the birdscanR package and set an output directory.
```{r}
library(birdscanR)

# Set main output directory
# =============================================================================
mainOutputDir = tempdir()
```

***
# Step 1: Extract the data from the SQL database

The data package is created from the output of `extractDbData()`. For a real
campaign, you extract the data from your database as described in the
vignette "Introduction to birdscanR". Extract all data of the campaign, with
all the echo features you want to publish:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Extract the data from the SQL database
# =============================================================================
dbData = extractDbData(
  dbDriverChar              = "SQL Server",
  dbServer                  = "MACHINE\\SERVERNAME",
  dbName                    = "CH_Sempach_2024",
  saveDbToFile              = TRUE,
  dbDataDir                 = mainOutputDir,
  radarTimeZone             = "Etc/GMT0",
  targetTimeZone            = "Etc/GMT0",
  listOfRfFeaturesToExtract = c(167, 168),
  siteLocation              = c(47.12764, 8.192569),
  sunOrCivil                = "civil",
  crepuscule                = "nauticalSolar"
)
```

In this vignette, we use the sample data extract that ships with the package:
two days (24-25 September 2024) of data from the radar at Sempach,
Switzerland.
```{r}
# Load example data
# =============================================================================
dbData = readRDS(system.file("extdata",
  "CH_Sempach_2024_SEP24_25_DataExtract.rds",
  package = "birdscanR"
))
dbName = "CH_Sempach_2024_SEP24_25"
```

***
# Step 2: (optional) Load the manual blind times

Manual blind times are periods in which the radar data should not be used,
e.g. because of rain or technical problems, that were noted by the radar
operator. They are stored in a csv file and loaded with
`loadManualBlindTimes()`. `createDataPackage()` merges them with the blind
times registered by the radar, so that the package holds one blind time table.

The csv file has one row per blind time and three columns without header:
start and stop time (`yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss`) and the type of blind time. The
package contains an example (`data(manualBlindTimes)`) with three blind times
during the sample data: rain on the morning of 24 September, a technical
outage in the night of 24-25 September, and clutter on the afternoon of 25
September. We write it to a csv file, as you would have it for a real
campaign, and load it:
```{r}
# Write the example manual blind times to a csv file (normally you already
# have this file)
# =============================================================================
data(manualBlindTimes)
manualBlindTimes
manualBlindTimesFile = file.path(mainOutputDir, "manualBlindTimes_Sempach.csv")
write.table(manualBlindTimes,
  file = manualBlindTimesFile, sep = ",",
  row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE
)

# Load the manual blind times
# =============================================================================
cManualBlindTimes = loadManualBlindTimes(
  filePath     = manualBlindTimesFile,
  blindTimesTZ = "Etc/GMT0",
  targetTZ     = "Etc/GMT0"
)
```
If there are no manual blind times, set `cManualBlindTimes = NULL`.

***
# Step 3: Describe the campaign in a metadata file

The description of the campaign is stored in a YAML file, one per campaign.
Write a template with `createDataPackageMetadataTemplate()` and fill it in with
a text editor:
```{r}
# Write the metadata template
# =============================================================================
metadataFile = file.path(mainOutputDir, "CH_Sempach_2024_metadata.yaml")
createDataPackageMetadataTemplate(filePath = metadataFile, overwrite = TRUE)
```

The template contains the following fields (shown here with the example
values of the template):
```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(metadataFile), sep = "\n")
```

A few points to consider when you fill it in:

- **campaignID**: `<country code>_<site>_<year>`, e.g. `CH_Sempach_2024`. It is
  used as the name of the package and of the output folder.
- **licenses**: `CC-BY-4.0` or `CC-BY-NC-4.0`.
- **embargo**: the date until which the data files stay restricted on Zenodo.
  The metadata (and thus the existence of the dataset, its contributors and
  how to contact them) are always public. If you leave it empty, the embargo
  ends 5 years after the last data in the package.
- **contributors**: list everyone who should get credit for the dataset. Each
  contributor needs one or more roles out of `ContactPerson`, `ProjectLeader`,
  `DataCollector`, `DataCurator`, `Researcher`, `RightsHolder` and
  `Supervisor`. At least one contributor must be the `ContactPerson`. Give the
  ORCID of each contributor whenever possible: it is used to merge the
  contributors of all campaigns into the creators of the collections.
- **embargoRequestType**: how a contributor wants to be involved when someone
  requests the data during the embargo: `1` = contact me (potential
  collaborator), `2` = citation only.

You can also build or adjust the metadata in R, and pass a list instead of a
file. Here, for example, we add a second contributor:
```{r}
# Adjust the metadata in R
# =============================================================================
metadata = yaml::read_yaml(metadataFile)
metadata$contributors[[2]] = list(
  title              = "Baptiste Schmid",
  givenName          = "Baptiste",
  familyName         = "Schmid",
  path               = "https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7736-7527",
  organization       = "Swiss Ornithological Institute",
  roles              = c("ProjectLeader", "DataCollector"),
  embargoRequestType = 1
)
```

The metadata are checked when the data package is created. If something is
missing or wrong, `createDataPackage()` stops and lists all problems, e.g.:
```{r, error = TRUE}
badMetadata = metadata
badMetadata$title = NULL
badMetadata$contributors[[2]]$roles = "Author"
createDataPackage(dbExtract = dbData, metadata = badMetadata)
```

***
# Step 4: Create the data package

`createDataPackage()` selects the data of the campaign, applies the filters you
set, and builds the data package. The filters are the same as in
`filterProtocolData()` and `filterEchoData()`; they are stored in the package
metadata, so users know how the data were selected. For a data package, you
normally keep all data of the campaign and only exclude what should not be
published (e.g. a test period at the start of the campaign).
```{r}
# Create the MR1 data package
# =============================================================================
dataPackage = createDataPackage(
  dbExtract         = dbData,
  metadata          = metadata,
  manualBlindTimes  = cManualBlindTimes,
  dbName            = dbName,
  timeRangeTargetTZ = c("2024-09-24 00:00", "2024-09-25 23:59"),
  outputDirPath     = mainOutputDir
)
dataPackage
```

## What is in the data package?

The package holds five tables (resources):

| Resource         | Content                                                                 |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `echo_data`      | Echoes, with their features, classification and MTR factors             |
| `protocol_data`  | Measurement periods (protocols) with their radar settings               |
| `blind_times`    | Periods in which the radar could not detect echoes                      |
| `sunrise_sunset` | Sunrise, sunset and twilight times at the site                          |
| `site_data`      | Location of the radar and radar/calibration parameters                  |

Read a table as a data frame with `frictionless::read_resource()`:
```{r}
# Read the blind times
# =============================================================================
blindTimes = frictionless::read_resource(dataPackage, "blind_times")
head(blindTimes)
table(blindTimes$type)
```

Each table has a schema that describes its columns, and how it links to the
other tables: each echo belongs to a measurement period (`protocolID`), and
each measurement period to a site (`siteID`).
```{r}
# Show the schema of the protocol table
# =============================================================================
protocolSchema = frictionless::get_schema(dataPackage, "protocol_data")
data.frame(
  name        = sapply(protocolSchema$fields, function(x) x$name),
  type        = sapply(protocolSchema$fields, function(x) x$type),
  description = sapply(protocolSchema$fields, function(x) x$description)
)
str(protocolSchema[c("primaryKey", "foreignKeys")])
```

Besides the metadata from the YAML file, `createDataPackage()` adds the
location and period of the campaign, the applied filters, the provenance of
the data (database, birdscanR and classifier versions), and a suggested
citation:
```{r}
# Show some of the package metadata
# =============================================================================
dataPackage$embargo
dataPackage$temporal
dataPackage$spatial
dataPackage$bibliographicCitation
str(dataPackage$`mr1dp:provenance`)
```

## The files on disk

Because we set `outputDirPath`, the package was written to a folder named after
the `campaignID`. This folder is what you upload to Zenodo:
```{r}
packageDir = file.path(mainOutputDir, "CH_Sempach_2024")
list.files(packageDir)
```

Anyone can read the package back, with R or any other software that supports
Frictionless Data Packages:
```{r}
# Read the data package from disk
# =============================================================================
dataPackageFromDisk = frictionless::read_package(file.path(packageDir, "datapackage.json"))
echoData = frictionless::read_resource(dataPackageFromDisk, "echo_data")
dim(echoData)
```

***
# Step 5: Validate the data package

Before you upload the package, check it with `validateDataPackage()`. It
checks the package metadata, that all tables are present and readable, that
the columns match their schema, that the keys between the tables are intact
(e.g. every echo belongs to an existing measurement period), and that the
content is plausible (e.g. start times before stop times, echoes within the
period of the package). Validate the files on disk, as these are what you
upload:
```{r}
# Validate the data package on disk
# =============================================================================
validation = validateDataPackage(packageDir)
validation
```

Errors mean that the package is incomplete or inconsistent: fix them before
you upload it. Warnings, e.g. a column without description, do not prevent
the upload. All issues are also available as a data frame in
`validation$issues`.

***
# Step 6: Upload the data package to Zenodo

The last step is to upload the data package to [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org).
`uploadDataPackageToZenodo()` uploads it as a **draft** record: it never
publishes the record. You check the draft on Zenodo, and publish it there
yourself.

## Zenodo account and token

You need a Zenodo account and a personal access token: on Zenodo, go to
*Account* > *Applications* > *Personal access tokens*, and create a token
with the scopes `deposit:write` and `deposit:actions`. The token gives access
to your Zenodo account, so never write it in a script. Store it as environment
variable `ZENODO_TOKEN` in your `.Renviron` file, which you can open with
`usethis::edit_r_environ()`:
```
ZENODO_TOKEN=<your token>
```
Restart R afterwards. `uploadDataPackageToZenodo()` reads the token from there.

## Test in the Zenodo sandbox first

The [Zenodo sandbox](https://sandbox.zenodo.org) is a copy of Zenodo for
testing: records there are not real and are removed regularly. It needs its
own account and token; store that token as `ZENODO_SANDBOX_TOKEN`. The BirdScan
MR1 community does not exist in the sandbox, so set `community = NULL`:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Upload the data package as draft to the Zenodo sandbox
# =============================================================================
draft = uploadDataPackageToZenodo(
  packageDir = packageDir,
  sandbox    = TRUE,
  community  = NULL
)
draft$url
```

## Upload to Zenodo

When the sandbox draft looks right, upload the package to Zenodo itself:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Upload the data package as draft to Zenodo
# =============================================================================
draft = uploadDataPackageToZenodo(packageDir = packageDir)
draft$url
draft$doi
```

`uploadDataPackageToZenodo()`:

1. validates the package with `validateDataPackage()`, and stops if it is not
   valid;
2. creates a draft record on Zenodo and reserves a DOI for it;
3. writes the DOI as `id` into the local `datapackage.json` and adds it to the
   suggested citation, so the published package carries its own DOI;
4. uploads `datapackage.json` and the CSV files;
5. fills in the metadata of the record from `datapackage.json`:

| Zenodo field          | Taken from                                                          |
|:----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Title, version        | `title`, `version`                                                  |
| Description           | `description`, site, period and suggested citation                 |
| Creators              | all contributors, with ORCID and affiliation                        |
| Contributors          | each contributor with each of their roles; the owner as rights holder |
| Licence               | `licenses`                                                          |
| Access                | embargoed until `embargo` (files restricted, metadata public), or open if the embargo has passed |
| Additional notes      | the contact person(s) for data requests during the embargo         |
| Keywords              | `keywords`                                                          |
| Related works         | `relatedIdentifiers`                                                |
| Locations, dates      | site coordinates, and the period of the data (`Collected`)         |
| Communities           | the BirdScan MR1 community (`birdscanmr1community`)                 |

## Publish the record

Open the draft (`draft$url`), check the metadata and files, and click
*Publish*. Publishing cannot be undone: the files of a published record can
no longer be changed, only replaced by a new version. On publication, Zenodo
registers the DOI, and sends the record to the curators of the BirdScan MR1
community for inclusion.

Finally, add the DOI as `id` to the metadata file of the campaign, so that new
versions of the package keep it:
```yaml
id: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.<record ID>
```

## Correct the data: upload a new version

Files of a published record cannot be changed. When the data of a campaign
are corrected, publish a **new version** instead. It gets its own DOI, and all
versions share the *concept DOI* of the record, which always points to the
latest version. Create the package again with:

- the DOI of the published record as `id` in the metadata file, and
- a higher `version`, e.g. `"1.0.1"` for a correction or `"2.0.0"` for a large
  change.

`uploadDataPackageToZenodo()` then sees the DOI and creates a draft of a new
version of that record, instead of a new record:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Upload a corrected data package as new version
# =============================================================================
draft = uploadDataPackageToZenodo(packageDir = packageDir)
draft$newVersion
draft$doi
```

The files of the previous version are replaced by the new ones. Links that
were added to the previous version on Zenodo, e.g. to the collection the
campaign belongs to (see below), are kept. Again, check the draft on Zenodo
and publish it there.

## Link records: add related identifiers

Metadata of a published record can be changed without a new version. To add
links to other records, such as an `IsPartOf` link from a campaign to the
owner collection it belongs to, use `addZenodoRelatedIdentifiers()`. It opens
an edit of the record and adds the links; existing links are kept, and links
the record already has are not added twice:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Link a campaign to its owner collection
# =============================================================================
addZenodoRelatedIdentifiers(
  doi = "https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.<record ID>",
  relatedIdentifiers = list(list(
    relationType      = "IsPartOf",
    relatedIdentifier = "https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.<collection record ID>"
  ))
)
```

By default, the edit is not published: check it on Zenodo and publish it
there. Use `publish = TRUE` to publish the edit directly; the DOI and version
of the record stay the same.

***
# Step 7: Group the campaigns in collections

A study that uses many campaigns should not have to cite each of them.
Campaigns are therefore grouped in **collections**, which are Zenodo records
with their own DOI:

- an **owner collection** groups the campaigns of one owner, e.g. all
  campaigns of the Swiss Ornithological Institute;
- the **community collection** groups the owner collections of the BirdScan
  MR1 community.

So, a study that uses up to 3 campaigns cites each campaign; with more than 3
campaigns, it cites their owner collections; with more than 3 owner
collections, it cites the community collection.

A collection record links to each member with a `HasPart` link, and each
member links back to the collection with `IsPartOf`. Both links use the
*concept DOI* (see above), so they stay valid when a campaign or collection gets
a new version. The record also holds the file `members.csv`, which lists the
members with the DOI, title and version of their latest version at the time of
the upload.

## Describe the collection

Like a campaign, a collection is described in a YAML file. Write the template,
and fill in the title, description, contributors (e.g. the curator of the
collection), the level (`owner` or `community`), and the DOIs of the published
member records:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Write the collection metadata template
# =============================================================================
collectionFile = file.path(mainOutputDir, "SOI_BirdScanMR1_collection.yaml")
createCollectionMetadataTemplate(filePath = collectionFile)
```

```yaml
collectionID: SOI_BirdScanMR1
level: owner
members:
  - https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.<campaign record ID>
  - https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.<campaign record ID>
```

## Upload the collection

`uploadCollectionToZenodo()` reads the latest version of each member from
Zenodo, and creates a draft of the collection record. It also adds an
`IsPartOf` link to the collection to each member, as an edit that is not
published yet:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Upload the collection as draft to Zenodo
# =============================================================================
draft = uploadCollectionToZenodo(metadata = collectionFile)
draft$members
draft$conceptDoi
```

Links can only be added to records of your own Zenodo account. Members of
other accounts (e.g. owner collections in the community collection) are listed
in a warning; their owners can add the link with
`addZenodoRelatedIdentifiers()`.

## Publish the collection, then the links

Check the draft on Zenodo and publish it. Then publish the `IsPartOf` links of
the members:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Publish the IsPartOf links of the members
# =============================================================================
linkCollectionMembers(doi = draft$doi, publish = TRUE)
```

Finally, add the DOI as `id` to the collection metadata file.

## Add campaigns: a new version of the collection

To add (or remove) campaigns, update `members` in the collection metadata
file and increase `version`. With the DOI of the collection as `id`,
`uploadCollectionToZenodo()` creates a new version of the collection, whose
`HasPart` links follow the new list of members. New members get their
`IsPartOf` link; publish these with `linkCollectionMembers()` after publishing
the new version.
